voiceover.text: So, what decides the strategies and tactics used on the day? A singles tennis player, mid-match, decides the plan isn't working and changes it completely. It takes about fifteen seconds, and nobody has to be told. A football team decides at half-time that its plan isn't working. Write down everything that has to happen before the new plan is actually being played, and roughly how long it takes. Then decide: does that make the team's tactics worse, or just different?

scenes.title: strategy and tactic, one level down

voiceover.text: Earlier you met the two words: the strategy is the plan for the whole contest, and tactics are the actions that serve it. Here they carry everything, so be exact. A tennis player's strategy might be to attack a weaker backhand, and one tactic is to serve wide to it. Every tactic is tested by one question: does it serve the strategy? If you'd do it once in a game, it's probably a tactic. If it describes the whole contest, it's a strategy.

Many factors shape how a plan is applied, and listing them earns less than grouping them. There are four families. First, you: your fitness, skills, experience, injuries, and for a team, cohesion, how well the group works together, and role clarity, everyone knowing their job. Those decide which strategies are even possible. A pressing game needs the fitness to sustain it. Second, the opponent: their strengths, weaknesses and patterns, found through opponent analysis. Third, the conditions: weather, wind, surface, venue, crowd, and the rules and how officials interpret them. Fourth, the state of the contest: the score, time left, fatigue, momentum, and what's at stake. Notice that you and the opponent are mostly known in advance. Conditions and the state of the contest aren't. That's why good plans carry contingencies.

The strongest answers take one factor and show it working differently in the two settings. Take changing the plan. For the tennis player, one person decides and acts, so it costs seconds. For a team, the change has to be decided, communicated, understood the same way by everyone, and then executed together. Until then, some players run the old plan and some the new one. That isn't worse tactics. It's the cost of eleven decision-makers. Teams manage it with structured flexibility: a few rehearsed alternatives, each with a name and a trigger, so a change means calling something the squad already owns. And teams have advantages too. They can run several tactics at once, and change players mid-game. So individuals adapt faster, but teams can run more at once.

scenes.title: the syllabus examples: conditions, and a group's strengths

voiceover.text: The syllabus names two factors, so work them. Environmental conditions first. A strong wind changes what's possible. A football team kicking with it might go long and shoot from range, then keep the ball low and short when kicking into it. A distance runner refuses to lead into a headwind, and sits behind someone instead. Then a group's strengths and weaknesses. Say a squad is fast but short. It should avoid aerial contests and play quick, low passes to feet, and pick an opponent's slow defence to run at. And notice how the two interact. The wind decides which of the group's strengths are usable on the day. A tall team that loves long balls might find them blown back at it.

The verb is discuss, so put the factors against each other. They often conflict. Exploit the opponent's weakness, or play to your own strength? Attack the weakness only if you can do it with a strength. Otherwise your strength usually wins, because a plan you can't carry out isn't a plan. Stick with the plan, or change it? Ask whether it's failing, or just not working yet. Change too early and you waste a good plan, too late and there's no time to recover. So set the trigger before the contest. And take a risk, or protect a lead? That depends on what's at stake and the time left. The same score late in a dead match and in an elimination final calls for different risks. Name the conflict, then say what resolves it.
Two things to remember. Individuals adapt faster, teams can run more at once. And name the conflict, then say what resolves it.

Two exam questions. First. A tennis player who normally attacks the net stays on the baseline all match on a slow, wet clay court. And a coach spots a clear weakness in the opposition's left-side defence, but doesn't target it, because both of the team's left-sided attackers are unavailable. For each, name the family of factor, the specific factor, and what it was traded against. Pause here to answer.

The tennis player's decision is driven by conditions, the slow wet surface, traded against their own strength at the net. The coach's decision is driven by the team itself, availability, traded against the opponent's weakness. Their strength couldn't attack it. The classic mistake is naming the factor without the trade-off.

scenes.title: attempt two (both losing, a third to go)

voiceover.text: Second. A badminton player is down six to fourteen in the deciding game. Their smash attack isn't working and they're tiring. A netball team trails by nine at three-quarter time, and its full-court press keeps being beaten by a long first pass. For each, what change would you make, what does it cost in that setting, how fast does it take effect, and what should have been prepared beforehand? Pause here to answer.

The badminton player can switch at once, to longer rallies and placement that save energy, but they're tired and alone. The netball team should drop to a zone that covers the long pass, but that needs the break and clear communication, and it's patchy at first. Both should have had a rehearsed plan B with a trigger. The classic mistake is inventing a new plan under pressure.

So place each decision at the level of strategy or tactic, sort the factors into their families, show how each plays out for one athlete and for a team, and weigh them against each other. One more factor is fully in the athlete's hands before they even arrive: what they eat and drink. What should athletes eat and drink, and when?
